newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe government in court over phone rules.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe government in court over phone rules.

text.p: A Zimbabwean firm on Thursday launched a court challenge against rules controlling private cellular phone operators, slamming them as unconstitutional and aimed at perpetuating the state's monopoly on the service.

In an application to the Supreme Court, T.S. Masiyiwa Holdings chairman Strive Masiyiwa charged that the manner in which the government enacted and implemented the rules showed vindictiveness towards him and violated his basic right to freedom of expression.

"The regulations are not designed to meet the objective of regulation but to prolong the monopoly (of the state Posts and Telecommunications Corporation)," said Wim Trengove, senior counsel for Masiyiwa.

"We submit that the evidence shows that the government and its departments is resentful and vindictive and has shown a determination to undermine his (the applicant's) effort to assert his right to freedom of expression," he said.

The government announced the new rules in February under which private firms wishing to operate a mobile cellular telephone service must apply for a licence from the minister of information, posts and telecommunications.
Anyone found operating without a licence faces a fine of up to Z$100,000 (U.S.$940), jail of up to two years or both.

The rules came a month after T.S. Masiyiwa won a historic court challenge to have the state monopoly on provision of mobile cellular telephones declared unconstitutional after it was denied a licence to operate such a service.

On Thursday, Trengrove and Adrian de Bourbon, also appearing for T.S. Masiyiwa, charged that the regulations were aimed at reinstating that monopoly, asking why it had taken so long to set up the processes to issue the licences.

The PTC launched last month its own cellular telephone service which it said would initially cover the southern African country's major cities of Harare, Bulawayo, Mutare and Kwekwe -- the areas Masiyiwa said in February his service was targeted at.
Appearing for the state, Attorney-General Patrick Chinamasa defended the regulations, saying the delay in issuing licences did not violate the constitution.

He said the regulations were an ad hoc measure, adding the government needed time to set up a more extensive regulatory framework which would not only cover private cellular telephone services but also the publicly switched network and broadcasting.
"All they do is introduce a regulatory framework, a licensing provision...They don't violate the constitution," he said.
